cards.title: Structured text
cards.html:
Structured text, abbreviated as ST or STX, is one of the five languages supported by the IEC 61131-3 standard, designed for programmable logic controllers (PLCs). It is a high-level language that is block structured and syntactically resembles Pascal, on which it is based. All of the languages share IEC61131 Common Elements. The variables and function calls are defined by the common elements so different languages within the IEC 61131-3 standard can be used in the same program.

Complex statements and nested instructions are supported:

  • Iteration loops (REPEAT-UNTIL; WHILE-DO)
  • Conditional execution (IF-THEN-ELSE; CASE)
  • Functions (SQRT(), SIN())

cards.title: Sample program
cards.html:
(* simple state machine *)
TxtState := STATES[StateMachine];

CASE StateMachine OF
   1: ClosingValve();
      StateMachine := 2;
   2: OpeningValve();
ELSE
    BadCase();
END_CASE;

Unlike in some other programming languages, there is no fall through for the CASE statement: the first matching condition is entered, and after running its statements, the CASE block is left without checking other conditions.

Additional ST programming examples

// PLC configuration
CONFIGURATION DefaultCfg
    VAR_GLOBAL
        b_Start_Stop  : BOOL;         // Global variable to represent a boolean.
        b_ON_OFF      : BOOL;         // Global variable to represent a boolean.
        Start_Stop AT %IX0.0:BOOL;    // Digital input of the PLC (Address 0.0)
        ON_OFF     AT %QX0.0:BOOL;    // Digital output of the PLC (Address 0.0). (Coil)
    END_VAR

    // Schedule the main program to be executed every 20 ms
    TASK Tick(INTERVAL := t#20ms);

    PROGRAM Main WITH Tick : Monitor_Start_Stop;
END_CONFIGURATION

PROGRAM Monitor_Start_Stop          // Actual Program
    VAR_EXTERNAL
        Start_Stop  : BOOL;
        ON_OFF      : BOOL;
    END_VAR
    VAR                             // Temporary variables for logic handling
        ONS_Trig    : BOOL;
        Rising_ONS  : BOOL;
    END_VAR

    // Start of Logic
    // Catch the Rising Edge One Shot of the Start_Stop input
    ONS_Trig    := Start_Stop AND NOT Rising_ONS;
    
    // Main Logic for Run_Contact -- Toggle ON / Toggle OFF ---
    ON_OFF := (ONS_Trig AND NOT ON_OFF) OR (ON_OFF AND NOT ONS_Trig);

    // Rising One Shot logic   
    Rising_ONS := Start_Stop;
END_PROGRAM

cards.title: Function block example
cards.html:
//=======================================================================
// Function Block Timed Counter :  Incremental count of the timed interval
//=======================================================================
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Timed_Counter
    VAR_INPUT
        Execute         : BOOL := FALSE;        // Trigger signal to begin Timed Counting
        Time_Increment  : REAL := 1.25;         // Enter Cycle Time (Seconds) between counts
        Count_Cycles    : INT  := 20;           // Number of Desired Count Cycles
    END_VAR
    
    VAR_OUTPUT
        Timer_Done_Bit  : BOOL := FALSE;        // One Shot Bit indicating Timer Cycle Done
        Count_Complete  : BOOL := FALSE;        // Output Bit indicating the Count is complete            
        Current_Count   : INT  := 0;            // Accumulating Value of Counter
    END_VAR
    
    VAR
        CycleTimer      : TON;                  // Timer FB from Command Library
        CycleCounter    : CTU;                  // Counter FB from Command Library
        TimerPreset     : TIME;                 // Converted Time_Increment in Seconds to MS
    END_VAR
        
    // Start of Function Block programming
    TimerPreset := REAL_TO_TIME(in := Time_Increment) * 1000;

    CycleTimer(
        in := Execute AND NOT CycleTimer.Q,
        pt := TimerPreset);

    Timer_Done_Bit := CycleTimer.Q;
    
    CycleCounter(
        cu := CycleTimer.Q,
        r := NOT Execute,
        pv := Count_Cycles);

    Current_Count := CycleCounter.cv;
    Count_Complete := CycleCounter.q;
    
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
cards.body: //======================================================================= // Function Block Timed Counter : Incremental count of the timed interval //======================================================================= FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Timed_Counter VAR_INPUT Execute : BOOL := FALSE; // Trigger signal to begin Timed Counting Time_Increment : REAL := 1.25; // Enter Cycle Time (Seconds) between counts Count_Cycles : INT := 20; // Number of Desired Count Cycles END_VAR VAR_OUTPUT Timer_Done_Bit : BOOL := FALSE; // One Shot Bit indicating Timer Cycle Done Count_Complete : BOOL := FALSE; // Output Bit indicating the Count is complete Current_Count : INT := 0; // Accumulating Value of Counter END_VAR VAR CycleTimer : TON; // Timer FB from Command Library CycleCounter : CTU; // Counter FB from Command Library TimerPreset : TIME; // Converted Time_Increment in Seconds to MS END_VAR // Start of Function Block programming TimerPreset := REAL_TO_TIME(in := Time_Increment) * 1000; CycleTimer( in := Execute AND NOT CycleTimer.Q, pt := TimerPreset); Timer_Done_Bit := CycleTimer.Q; CycleCounter( cu := CycleTimer.Q, r := NOT Execute, pv := Count_Cycles); Current_Count := CycleCounter.cv; Count_Complete := CycleCounter.q; END_FUNCTION_BLOCK

cards.title: IEC 61131-3
cards.html:
IEC 61131-3 is the third part (of 10) of the international standard IEC 61131 for programmable logic controllers. It was first published in December 1993 by the IEC; the current (fourth) edition was published in May 2025.

Part 3 of IEC 61131 deals with basic software architecture and programming languages of the control program within PLC. The current edition defines three graphical and one textual programming language standards:

  • Ladder diagram (LD), graphical
  • Function block diagram (FBD), graphical
  • Structured text (ST), textual
  • Sequential function chart (SFC), has elements to organize programs for sequential and parallel control processing, graphical.

Previous editions also included:

  • Instruction list (IL), textual. Deprecated in the third edition (2013) and removed in the fourth edition (2025).

cards.title: Elementary Data Types (basic)
cards.html:
• Bit Strings – groups of on/off values
    • BOOL - 1 bit (0,1)
    • BYTE – 8 bit (1 byte)
    • WORD – 16 bit (2 byte)
    • DWORD – 32 bit (4 byte)
    • LWORD – 64 bit (8 byte)
  • INTEGER – whole numbers (Considering byte size 8 bits)
    • SINT – signed short integer (1 byte)
    • INT – signed integer (2 byte)
    • DINT – signed double integer (4 byte)
    • LINT – signed long integer (8 byte)
    • USINT – Unsigned short integer (1 byte)
    • UINT – Unsigned integer (2 byte)
    • UDINT – Unsigned double integer (4 byte)
    • ULINT – Unsigned long integer (8 byte)
  • REAL – floating point IEC 60559 (same as IEEE 754-2008)
    • REAL – (4 byte)
    • LREAL – (8 byte)

cards.title: Elementary Data Types (Date and Time)
cards.html:
Duration literals
Unit Description
d Day
h Hour
m Minute
s Second
ms Millisecond
us Microsecond
ns Nanosecond
  • Duration
    • TIME – (implementer specific). Literals in the form of T#5m90s15ms
    • LTIME – (8 byte). Literals extend to nanoseconds in the form of T#5m90s15ms542us15ns
  • Date
    • DATE – calendar date (implementer specific)
    • LDATE – calendar date (8 byte, nanoseconds since 1970-01-01, restricted to multiple of one day)
  • Time of day
    • TIME_OF_DAY / TOD – clock time (implementer specific)
    • LTIME_OF_DAY / LTOD – clock time (8 byte)
  • Date and time of Day
    • DATE_AND_TIME / DT – time and date (implementer specific)
    • LDATE_AND_TIME / LDT – time and date (8 byte, nanoseconds since 1970-01-01)

cards.title: Elementary Data Types (Character / Character string)
cards.html:
STRING escape sequences
Escape sequence Produces
$$ $
$' '
$L linefeed
$N newline
$P page (form feed)
$R return
$T tab
$xx hex value
  • Existing
    • CHAR – Single-byte character (1 byte, limited to characters 0 to 255 of ISO/IEC 10646)
    • WCHAR – Double-byte character (2 byte, limited to characters 0 to 65535 of ISO/IEC 10646)
    • STRING – Variable-length single-byte character string. Literals specified with single quote, 'This is a STRING Literal'
    • WSTRING – Variable-length double-byte character string. Literals specified with a double quote, "This is a WSTRING Literal"
  • New in version 4 of the standard
    • UCHAR – Single character encoded according to UTF-8
    • USTRING - Variable-length character string in which each character is encoded according to UTF-8

cards.title: Generic Data Types
cards.html:
Only available for the input / output/ in-out variables of system-defined Program Organization Units (POUs, see below)

  • ANY
  • ANY_DERIVED
  • ANY_ELEMENTARY
    • ANY_MAGNITUDE
      • ANY_NUM
        • ANY_REAL: LREAL, REAL
        • ANY_INT
          • ANY_UNSIGNED: ULINT, UDINT, UINT, USINT
          • ANY_SIGNED: LINT, DINT, INT, SINT
      • ANY_DURATION: TIME, LTIME
    • ANY_BIT: LWORD, DWORD, WORD, BYTE, BOOL
    • ANY_CHARS
      • ANY_STRING: STRING, WSTRING
      • ANY_CHAR: CHAR, WCHAR
    • ANY_DATE: DATE_AND_TIME (DT), DATE_AND_TIME(LDT), DATE, TIME_OF_DAY (TOD), LTIME_OF_DAY(LTOD)

User-defined Data Types

  • Enumerated data type
  • Enumerated data type with named value
  • Subrange data type – puts limits on value i.e., INT(4 .. 20) for current
  • Array data type – multiple values stored in the same variable.
  • Structured data type – composite of several variables and types.
  • Directly derived data type – type derived from one of the above types to give new name and initial value as a type.
  • References – a kind of strongly typed pointer. Arithmetic operation of the value of this type is prohibited.

cards.title: Variables
cards.html:
Variable attributes: RETAIN, CONSTANT, AT

  • Global
  • Direct (local)
  • I/O Mapping – Input, Output, I/O
  • External
  • Temporary

Configuration

  • Resource – Like a CPU
  • Tasks – Can be multiple per CPU.
  • Programs – Can be executed once, on a timer, on an event.

Program organization unit (POU)

  • Functions
    • Standard: ADD, SQRT, SIN, COS, GT, MIN, MAX, AND, OR, etc.
    • Custom
  • Function Blocks
    • Standard:
    • Custom – Libraries of functions can be supplied by a vendor or third party.
  • Programs

Configuration, resources, tasks

  • Configuration – processing resources, memory for IO, execution rates, number of tasks.

Object oriented programming (OOP)

  • The 3rd revision of the standard describes how to implement OOP within the application programming

cards.q: In IEC 61131-3 Structured Text, which line sets a variable?
cards.why: ST uses := for assignment and = for comparison, as Pascal does. Siemens calls its version SCL.

cards.q: Why is a WHILE loop that waits for an input to change a mistake in a PLC?
options: WHILE is not allowed in ST
cards.why: The input image is read at the start of each scan, so inside the loop it never changes: the scan never ends and the watchdog stops the PLC. Wait across scans with a state or a timer instead.

cards.q: When is Structured Text a better choice than ladder?
options: Simple interlocks an electrician must read
cards.why: Arithmetic, arrays, string handling and loops are clumsy in ladder and short in ST. Plain interlocks stay easier to read and fault-find in ladder.

cards.q: Which of these is not one of IEC 61131-3's programming languages?
cards.why: The standard defines Ladder Diagram, Function Block Diagram, Structured Text and Sequential Function Chart (Instruction List was dropped in the 2013 edition). Some PLCs run other languages alongside, but outside the standard.

cards.q: Write the logic, in Structured Text, for a clamp: when Start is pressed, close the clamp; when ClampClosed comes on, run the drill for 3 s; then open the clamp and wait for ClampOpen.

steps.ask: How to hold where the sequence is
steps.show: An integer `Step`, with `CASE Step OF … END_CASE`
`20: CloseClamp := TRUE; IF ClampClosed THEN Step := 30; END_IF`
`30: Drill := TRUE; DrillTimer(IN := TRUE, PT := T#3S); IF DrillTimer.Q THEN Step := 40; END_IF`
`40: CloseClamp := FALSE; Drill := FALSE; IF ClampOpen THEN Step := 10; END_IF`, with the timer reset (IN := FALSE) outside step 30

cards.why: Each step sets its outputs and waits for one condition to move on. Outputs written inside the CASE stay as last written, so outputs are often set from the step number after the CASE instead (Drill := Step = 30), which cannot leave one stuck on.

cards.q: `IF StartButton THEN Count := Count + 1; END_IF` counts far too many presses. What fixes it?
options: Put it in a faster task
cards.why: The IF is true on every scan the button is held: hundreds of counts per press. An R_TRIG block gives TRUE for one scan when its input goes from FALSE to TRUE.
